body_html:
Came here from TikTok? This is the longer version: all 10 foods, why each one helps, how much to eat, easy swaps, and what to skip.

Gaining muscle comes down to three things: lifting something heavy enough to challenge you, eating enough protein spread across the day, and eating enough total food that your body has material to build with. Skip any one of them and progress stalls. No food builds muscle on its own, and no powder or pill replaces the other two.

The good news is that the best foods for gaining muscle are ordinary groceries. Below are the 10 we would put in any cart, with a normal portion, rough protein grams, and a simple way to eat each one.

How Much Protein You Need to Gain Muscle

A common target in sports nutrition for people who lift is roughly 0.7 grams of protein per pound of body weight per day (about 1.6 g per kg). For a 160-pound person that is about 110 to 115 grams a day. If you have a lot of weight to lose, base it on your goal weight instead.

  • Split it up: 25–40 g at each of 3–4 meals works better than one huge dinner.
  • Eat a little more than you burn: a small surplus (a snack or an extra portion of carbs a day) is enough. A big surplus mostly adds fat.
  • Lift 2–4 times a week: the food gives your body the materials; training is what tells it to build.

Portions and grams below are rough guides for healthy adults. If you have kidney disease, diabetes or another medical condition, check a big jump in protein with your doctor or a registered dietitian first.

The 10 Best Foods to Gain Muscle Mass

1. Eggs

3 large eggs: about 18 g protein. Cheap, quick and complete. The yolk carries about half the egg's protein plus vitamin D and choline, so eat the whole egg. Scramble 3 eggs with spinach, or hard-boil a batch on Sunday for the week.

2. Chicken Breast or Thigh

4 oz cooked: about 30–35 g protein. The easiest way to hit 30 g in one meal. Thighs have a bit more fat and stay juicier; both work. Cook 2 pounds at once and use it in bowls, wraps and salads.

3. Greek Yogurt (Plain)

1 cup: about 20–23 g protein. Roughly twice the protein of regular yogurt. Buy plain and add berries and a drizzle of honey yourself; flavored cups often carry as much sugar as a dessert. Great as a breakfast or a bedtime snack.

4. Salmon and Other Fatty Fish

4 oz cooked salmon: about 25 g protein. Adds omega-3 fats that most people don't get enough of. Canned salmon, sardines and trout count too and cost less. Aim for fish twice a week.

5. Lean Beef

4 oz cooked 90% lean ground beef or sirloin: about 25–28 g protein. Also one of the best food sources of iron, zinc and vitamin B12, which matter when you are training hard. Use it in tacos, chili or a rice bowl.

6. Cottage Cheese

1 cup: about 25 g protein. One of the highest-protein foods per calorie in the dairy case. Eat it with fruit, blend it into pancake batter, or stir it into pasta sauce to make it creamy. Watch the sodium if you eat it daily.

7. Beans and Lentils

1 cup cooked lentils: about 18 g protein; 1 cup black beans: about 15 g. Protein plus fiber and slow carbs that fuel your workouts. Pair them with rice or a grain at the same meal or during the day to round out the protein. Add fiber slowly and drink water.

8. Tofu, Tempeh and Edamame

Half a block of firm tofu (about 7 oz): about 20 g protein. 1 cup shelled edamame: about 18 g. Soy is one of the few plant foods with complete protein, which makes it the go-to for vegetarians who lift. Press tofu, cube it, and roast or pan-fry until crisp.

9. Milk (or Soy Milk)

1 cup: about 8 g protein. An easy way to add protein and calories without another meal. A tall glass with dinner, or a smoothie of milk, banana, peanut butter and oats, adds 20+ g of protein to a day. Unsweetened soy milk has about the same protein; most almond and oat milks have very little.

10. Oats, Rice and Potatoes

1 cup cooked oats: about 6 g protein; 1 cup rice: about 4–5 g. These are on the list for the carbs, not the protein. Carbs refill the energy your muscles burn while lifting, so you can train harder and recover. If you are trying to gain and can't, this is usually where the missing food is.

Easy Add-Ons That Help

  • Peanut butter, nuts and seeds: 2 tbsp peanut butter has about 7–8 g protein and lots of calories in a small space. Handy if you struggle to eat enough.
  • Canned tuna: about 20–25 g protein per can, no cooking.
  • Bananas and other fruit: quick carbs before a workout, plus potassium.
  • Olive oil and avocado: healthy fats that make meals more filling and add calories without volume.

If You Struggle to Eat Enough

Some people, often called hard gainers, simply fill up fast. A few tricks help without forcing huge plates:

  • Drink some of your food: a smoothie with milk, a banana, oats and peanut butter goes down far easier than a third meal.
  • Add calorie-dense extras: olive oil on vegetables, cheese on eggs, nuts on yogurt.
  • Eat on a schedule: set 4 meal times instead of waiting until you feel hungry.
  • Keep easy protein on hand: boiled eggs, cottage cheese cups, tuna pouches and cooked chicken in the fridge.

A Simple Muscle-Gain Day (About 120 g Protein)

  • Breakfast: 3 scrambled eggs, 1 cup oats cooked in milk, a banana (about 30 g)
  • Lunch: chicken, rice and black bean bowl with salsa (about 40 g)
  • Snack: 1 cup Greek yogurt with berries and a handful of nuts (about 25 g)
  • Dinner: 4 oz salmon, a baked potato and roasted vegetables (about 28 g)

Scale portions up or down for your size and goal. A glass of milk with dinner or a peanut butter sandwich before bed is an easy way to add more.

Simple Swaps

  • Flavored yogurt → plain Greek yogurt with fruit (more protein, less sugar)
  • Sugary cereal → oats with milk and peanut butter
  • Chips → roasted edamame or a handful of nuts
  • Fried chicken sandwich → grilled chicken wrap
  • Energy drink before the gym → a banana and a glass of milk

For more trades like these, see our healthy swaps for sugar cravings.

What to Skip

  • "Mass gainer" tubs as your main food: many are mostly sugar. Real meals plus a homemade smoothie do the same job.
  • Dirty bulking: eating everything in sight adds fat much faster than muscle. A small surplus is enough.
  • Protein only at dinner: spread it out over the day.
  • Skipping carbs: low-carb eating makes hard training feel harder and slows recovery for most people.
  • Lots of alcohol: it gets in the way of sleep and recovery.
  • Supplements sold as a shortcut: no pill builds muscle. Food, lifting and sleep do.

Not sure you are eating enough protein now? These signs you aren't eating enough protein are a quick check.

Sleep Is Part of the Plan

Muscle is built while you recover, not while you lift. Most adults need 7–9 hours of sleep. If you eat well and train hard but sleep 5 hours a night, progress will be slower than it should be.

Why a List Isn't Enough

Most people who "can't gain muscle" are eating less protein and less food than they think. A list tells you what to buy; it doesn't tell you that Tuesday you hit 60 g instead of 110. faq.q: What foods help you gain muscle fast?
faq.a: Eggs, chicken, Greek yogurt, fish, lean beef, cottage cheese, beans, tofu and milk give you protein, and oats, rice and potatoes give you the energy to train. Muscle still builds slowly; lifting regularly and eating enough are what move it.

faq.q: How much protein do I need to build muscle?
faq.a: A common target for people who lift is about 0.7 g per pound of body weight a day (about 1.6 g per kg), split over 3 to 4 meals. If you have a medical condition such as kidney disease, check with your doctor first.

faq.q: Can you build muscle without protein powder?
faq.a: Yes. Powder is just a convenient protein source. Eggs, dairy, meat, fish, beans and soy can cover your needs with normal meals.

faq.q: Do I need to eat more calories to gain muscle?
faq.a: Usually a little. A small surplus, like one extra snack or a bigger portion of rice or potatoes a day, supports muscle gain. A large surplus mostly adds fat.

bottom_line: The best foods to gain muscle mass are everyday groceries: eggs, chicken, Greek yogurt, fish, lean beef, cottage cheese, beans, soy, milk, and plenty of oats, rice and potatoes. Aim for roughly 0.7 g of protein per pound of body weight spread over your meals, eat a little more than you burn, lift 2 to 4 times a week and sleep well. Do that consistently and the muscle follows.
